title: Good Data, Bad Data
desc: Clean and sort data to see how the quality of data shapes what AI learns
content_html:
What You'll Do

AI learns from data, so the data has to be fair and complete for the AI to be any good. Bad data in means bad decisions out — an AI is only ever as good as what it learns from. In this project you'll gather some data yourself, then deliberately break it, so you can see exactly how gaps and bias in the data turn into gaps and bias in the AI.

You'll Need

  • A whiteboard or paper to tally results
  • A simple question to survey people around you (for example "What is your favourite fruit?")
  • Optional: a few printed photos or a short list to act as a "training set" to sort

Steps

  1. Survey everyone you can (your class, your group) and tally the results. This is your "good" dataset — everyone got a say.
  2. Interrogate it: did everyone get to answer? Was anyone away or skipped? Is any group over- or under-counted?
  3. Now break it on purpose: imagine you only asked the front two rows. Predict how the result would change, then work out why that sample is unfair.
  4. Connect it to AI: if this biased survey trained an AI to "guess the class's favourite fruit," what wrong thing would it learn?
  5. Write three rules for collecting fairer, more complete data next time.

Examples

  • A face-unlock trained mostly on one skin tone works poorly for everyone else.
  • A voice assistant trained on one accent keeps mishearing people who speak differently.
  • A "best student" predictor trained only on past winners quietly repeats old unfairness.

Tips

  • Spot the bias yourself by always asking "who is missing?"
  • Keep the fruit example light, then pivot to the real-world examples — that's where the stakes land.
  • Remember bad data is usually an honest mistake, not villainy — which is exactly why checking it is everyone's job.

Think About It

  • What does "fair and complete" data actually mean for a dataset?
  • How could a company end up with biased data without meaning to?
  • If you found an AI was trained on unfair data, what would you do about it?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Clean a deliberately messy list (duplicates, blanks, typos) and explain each fix.
  • Medium: Find a real news story about AI bias and summarise what data caused it.
  • Hard: Design a data-collection plan for a fair "favourite school lunch" predictor — who you'd ask, how many, and how you'd avoid bias.
